questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A join that returned too many rows
questions.learningObjective: Explain the impact of row explosion on aggregates
questions.stem: Historical case: analyst Idris sees inflated revenue after a join

options.text: Stage one: switch to a left join; stage two: recompute
options.misconception: thinks join type fixes non-unique keys

options.text: Stage one: accept the inflated total; stage two: report it
options.misconception: accepts an inflated aggregate

options.text: Stage one: check join key uniqueness; stage two: deduplicate before summing
Stage one: drop revenue; stage two: report counts only
options.misconception: discards the metric instead of fixing the join

questions.explanation: Checking key uniqueness and deduplicating before summing fixes the root cause. Accepting inflated totals, switching join types, or dropping the metric does not.

questions.topic: What a log does to a range
questions.learningObjective: Explain why log is used for multiplicative processes
questions.stem: Historical case: a note models multiplicative growth over time

options.text: Multiplicative growth cannot be modelled at all
options.misconception: denies the possibility of modelling growth

options.text: Log makes growth additive in the wrong direction
options.misconception: misstates the direction of linearisation

options.text: Log is only for normalising units, not growth
options.misconception: restricts log to unit normalisation

options.text: Log linearises multiplicative growth, enabling linear models

questions.explanation: Log transforms multiplicative growth into additive linear form, enabling linear models. It does not misdirect, serve only units, or make growth unmodelable.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Arithmetic mean against geometric mean
questions.learningObjective: Explain when arithmetic mean overstates growth
questions.stem: Historical case: a note averages volatile annual returns

options.text: The arithmetic mean always equals compounded growth
options.misconception: ignores volatility's effect on compounding

options.text: The arithmetic mean overstates compounded growth when returns vary
The geometric mean overstates growth in all cases
options.misconception: reverses the overstatement

options.text: Variance has no effect on the mean comparison
options.misconception: denies variance's role in the gap

questions.explanation: With volatile returns the arithmetic mean exceeds the compounded growth rate. The geometric mean captures compounding, and variance drives the gap between the means.
questions.hint: Volatility widens the gap between means.

questions.stem: Historical case: a join returned 150 rows from a 100-row left table

answer.exemplar: Some left rows matched multiple right rows because the join key was not unique on the right side, multiplying rows.

options.text: Stage one: the data is normal; stage two: arithmetic mean is wrong
options.misconception: blames the arithmetic mean for normal data

options.text: Stage one: the data is constant; stage two: means should match

questions.learningObjective: Explain how to build a leakage-free rolling feature
questions.stem: Historical case: analyst Nia needs a cumulative feature per customer over time

options.text: Stage one: shuffle rows; stage two: cumulative aggregate in random order
options.misconception: destroys temporal order and leaks future rows

options.text: Stage one: compute the global aggregate; stage two: broadcast to all rows
options.misconception: leaks global information into every row

options.text: Stage one: sort by date; stage two: cumulative aggregate using only prior rows
Stage one: use future rows; stage two: assign to past rows
